sampling_model.design: Randomized binary treatment with known allocation probability \(\pi\in[\pi_0,1-\pi_0]\).
sampling_model.units: Independent draws of \(O=(A,X,Y)\) from the observed Gaussian law \(P_{\vartheta}\) indexed by \(\vartheta\in\Theta\); ordinary Wald inference is restricted to \(\Theta_+(\nu_*)\), while projection inference and the angular frontier retain their stated whole-class domains.
sampling_model.overlap: The allocation probability is uniformly separated from zero and one.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: The finite-dimensional map \(\theta(P)\) is estimated from arm-specific means, variances, and outcome-covariances and the pooled covariate covariance on an evaluation split independent of covariate selection.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: Within the underlying conditional-optimal-transport information model, covariates monotonically tighten partial-identification bounds and variable selection is left as a future direction; the compact-support assumptions of particular theorems are a separate restriction.
Sparse covariance eigenvalues lower-bound the regression submodularity ratio and yield a forward-selection approximation guarantee.
Submodularity ratio and generalized curvature jointly yield a tight generic cardinality-constrained greedy guarantee.
Multiplier-bootstrap aggregation permits valid covariate and model selection among conditional-transport dual bounds.
A smooth-density quadratic conditional-transport estimator has a fixed-target central limit theorem away from equality.
A short never-empty confidence interval is valid when estimated lower and upper bounds have a regular joint Gaussian limit.

body.tldr: For a randomized Gaussian experiment, retaining a subset of pretreatment covariates raises the sharp conditional-optimal-transport lower endpoint for the mean squared individual treatment effect. Each endpoint increment equals a squared chordal distance between upper-hemisphere lifts of two residualized arm-score vectors. A sparse Schur-complement frame bound and a hemisphere Lipschitz comparison imply \(\gamma_k\ge(m/M)(s/V)\), so forward greedy attains a dimension-free fraction of the best size-\(k\) tightening. A fully specified randomized unequal-scale observed-data family approaches \(k/[1+(k-1)(M/m)(V/s)]\), proving that both margin factors are necessary and that the dimension-free certificate is optimal as the budget varies. On the compact image \(\Theta\), independent evaluation yields credited conditional Wald inference on the separated subclass \(\Theta_+(\nu_*)\) and a conservative raw-moment projection interval over all of \(\Theta\), including equality. The exact fixed-\(k\) frontier remains an explicit open problem.

project_justification.gap: Conditional optimal transport supplies sharp covariate-assisted causal bounds, but existing work treats the conditioning set as fixed. Generic weak-submodularity theory does not determine the approximation ratio of the unequal-scale two-arm Gaussian endpoint.
project_justification.niche: The Gaussian endpoint has a residual-score geometry that is absent from one-response regression: singleton and joint gains are chordal distances observed through a sparse Schur-complement frame.
project_justification.fill: The project derives that geometry, proves the optimal dimension-free margin certificate with a fully randomized unequal-scale lower family, transfers it to greedy selection, and formulates credited sample-split Wald inference on \(\Theta_+(\nu_*)\) together with projection inference on the full compact moment image \(\Theta\).

body.related_work: Lin, Gao, Blanchet, and Glynn (2025) motivate covariate-assisted conditional transport, prove interpolation toward the conditional bound, give Gaussian benchmarks, and identify variable selection as future work. Their AISTATS paper (2026) establishes sharp fixed-information bounds and adapted-Wasserstein estimation, while their smooth-density paper (2026) gives rates and a fixed-target quadratic central limit theorem. Das and Kempe (2011) introduce the submodularity ratio and its sparse-spectral control for regression; Bian et al. (2017) and Elenberg et al. (2018) provide generic greedy and restricted-curvature machinery. Ji, Lei, and Spector (2023) already establish selection-valid inference among covariate and model choices, so that principle is not positioned as new. Gelbrich (1990) and Fang and Zhu (2020) explain why covariance transport geometry extends to some elliptical laws but not automatically through conditioning. Imbens and Manski (2004) and Stoye (2021) motivate honest inference at delicate partial-identification boundaries; the present projection interval uses their lesson without claiming a new length-optimal procedure.
body.technical_internal_limitation: The sharpness family has a positive but vanishing endpoint contrast as \(h\downarrow0\), which is legitimate for a ratio frontier but does not establish a worst-case greedy-value ratio at a fixed signal amplitude. Ordinary Wald inference is asserted only on \(\Theta_+(\nu_*)\); equality laws satisfy \(b_S=0\) and \(\nu_S^2=0\) and are handled by whole-image projection. Computing the best sparse margins may itself be combinatorial, so the theorem accepts certified values of \(m,M,s,V\) as inputs.
body.honest_scope: The dimension-free certificate, its two-factor necessity, and the greedy consequence are theorem targets over the explicitly quantified Gaussian law classes. The extremal construction specifies the covariate law, independent arm noises, independent \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) assignment, potential outcomes, and observed outcome. Sample-split Wald coverage on \(\Theta_+(\nu_*)\) and conservative projection coverage on all of \(\Theta\), including equality laws, are credited finite-dimensional inference specializations rather than novelty claims. The exact fixed-\(k\) lower frontier and any locally shortest equality-boundary interval remain open. When \(k=1\), every positive submodularity ratio equals one and greedy is optimal. On the equal-scale slice \(v_0=v_1\) and \(c_1=-c_0\), the gain reduces to the classical regression explained-variance objective, recovering the known sparse-spectral setting. When \(R=1\), all covariate-outcome covariances vanish and \(F\equiv0\), so the ratio convention returns one.
